title: 5 Great Technical Documentation Examples (And What You Can Learn From Them)
summary: These technical API documentation examples are detailed, well-organized, and interactive, helping you spend less time handling support requests.
body_text: 5 Great Technical Documentation Examples (And What You Can Learn From Them) The person who writes API documentation is almost never the person who uses it. That's a problem because the team writing it knows the API cold. They built it, they named every endpoint, and the structure that feels obvious to them is the structure they reach for. The developer reading it has none of that context, and what's obvious to the author is a dead end for them. The best technical documentation is written for that outside developer. That means structuring the docs around what the reader is trying to do, anticipating where they'll get stuck, and showing the path through a task instead of listing the parts and trusting them to assemble it. This piece walks through five examples of great technical API documentation. For each one, we break down what it does to write for the reader, so you have something concrete to benchmark your own docs against. 1. API Reference An API reference walks developers through all the endpoints, parameters, and response codes needed to interact with your API. A detailed one saves you from answering the same troubleshooting questions over and over, and lets developers actually use everything your API can do instead of guessing at it. API Reference Example: Socure Socure's reference for the " Start an Evaluation " endpoint never assumes you already know how the API is organized. A plain-language line at the top tells you what the endpoint does before you hit a single parameter. Then, instead of dumping every field for all eight evaluation types onto one page, it lets you pick your workflow and shows only the schema that applies to you. The page also does the copying work for you. A language switcher renders the request in Shell, Java, Python, Node, or Go, so you copy something that runs in your stack instead of translating from cURL in your head. What You Can Learn Summarize what the endpoint is for at the top of the page, in plain language. Let readers narrow to their use case before showing them a schema. Provide real code examples in the languages your developers actually use. Get the reference right, and a developer can self-serve from the first visit. But a reference assumes they already know what they're trying to do. A getting started guide is what gets them there. 2. Getting Started Guide Your getting started guide should walk new users through the entire setup, addressing any problems they may encounter along the way and introducing them to the structure of your service. Getting Started Guide Example: Gusto Gusto’s getting started guide works, first and foremost, because it’s well-organized. It follows a chronological, step-by-step structure and includes an interactive table of contents, so a developer can jump straight to the step they're stuck on instead of scrolling to find it. From there, the guide stays with the developer through each step. The code examples come in both cURL and JavaScript, so they copy the call that matches their stack instead of rewriting it, and every step shows what the endpoint returns, so they can confirm they're on track before moving on, or catch a wrong response early. When the quickstart path isn't enough, the guide links out to deeper resources like the full Employee Onboarding guide. The result is a guide that meets developers wherever they are, whether they're cruising through setup or stuck on a single step. What You Can Learn Order the steps the way a developer will actually work through them. Show what each endpoint returns so readers can check their progress. Give code in more than one language. Link out to deeper guides for readers who need them. A getting started guide has one job: get a new developer to their first working call without losing them along the way. Gusto does it by removing the friction at every step. Whatever you're building, your guide should anticipate potential issues before they happen, so your developers can move quickly and build with confidence. 3. Tutorial A tutorial helps developers build a specific project or master a concept integral to your API. It should open by telling the reader what the tutorial covers, what state they need to be in before they start, and any other prerequisites. From there, it moves step by step, showing the expected result at each stage so the reader always knows whether they're on track. Tutorial Example: Clever Clever's Example OAuth/OIDC Walkthrough works because it assumes you'll hit friction and clears it before you do. That starts before step one: it flags the required subscription and lists the two prerequisites (a Clever dev app and Postman) up top, so no one gets three steps in before discovering they're missing a tool. From there, it walks the full OAuth flow one stage at a time, with section headers, screenshots, and a worked example at each step, so the reader can match what's on their screen against what should be happening. The friction-clearing continues mid-flow. The walkthrough warns that the authorization code expires after a minute and has you set up the Postman query in advance, so a first-timer doesn't lose the code to the clock. A clickable table of contents sits at the top and side of the page for skipping around, and a recent last-updated date tells the reader the steps still reflect how the API works today. What You Can Learn List prerequisites up front, before the reader has invested any time. Walk one stage at a time, and show the expected result at each step. Clear friction before the reader hits it, like a warning about a code that expires. Show a recent last-updated date so readers trust the steps still work. Clever's walkthrough clears friction because someone knew where the friction was. You can find the same map in your support tickets: the questions that come up again and again are the steps your tutorial is failing to cover. Start there, fix the spot that generates the most tickets, and work down the list. 4. Changelog A changelog lists every bug fix, update, and new feature, in order, so developers can see what changed and when. Done well, it's how a developer catches the update that affects their integration before it breaks something. Changelog Example: Doppler Doppler's changelog works because it respects the reader's time. Entries are grouped by month and written as short, plain-language bullets, so a developer can scan a release at a glance instead of parsing paragraphs. Each one says what changed and what it now lets you do, not just that something moved. For example, the activity-log update doesn't only announce multiple destinations; it spells out that you can now configure separate webhook endpoints for Slack, Discord, Teams, and Generic HTTPS, each with its own credentials. The reader comes away knowing the new capability, not just that a release happened. It also keeps that scannability without losing depth by linking out. Nearly every entry links to the full documentation page for the feature it mentions, so a developer who's affected can click through for the details while everyone else keeps scanning. The entries also flag who a change is for, calling out Enterprise customers by name, so readers can skip what doesn't apply to them. What You Can Learn Order changes by date so readers can find what's new since they last checked. Keep each entry short and in plain language. Tell readers what each change lets them do, not just what changed. Link every change to the page that explains it in full. Say who a change affects so readers can skip what doesn't apply. A changelog is the one doc developers check to find out what your last release means for them. Most teams write it for themselves, a log of what shipped. Doppler writes it for the reader: every entry answers "does this affect me, and what can I do now." Write yours the same way, and the changelog stops being a record of your work and becomes a tool for theirs. 5. Developer Guide A developer guide helps a developer integrate with or build on your API, walking through real tasks with step-by-step instructions and code examples. Where a getting started guide gets someone to their first call, a developer guide covers the full lifecycle of working with a resource. Developer Guide Example: Samsara Read Samsara's Drivers guide , and you come away knowing not just how to call the API, but how it behaves when you push on it. It opens with the exact scopes you need ( Read Drivers , Write Drivers ), then walks the full lifecycle of a driver, create, retrieve, list, update, deactivate, with a copy-ready cURL request and a real example response for each one, so a developer can see the shape of what they'll get back before they run anything. What sets it apart is that it tells you where the API will surprise you. You can't actually delete a driver, only deactivate them, because Samsara preserves their history for compliance. The eldSettings field is read-only, so the guide shows the specific override you have to use instead. List calls return only active drivers unless you ask otherwise. These are the details a developer would otherwise discover by hitting an error, and the guide gets to them first. What You Can Learn State the required scopes or permissions before the first call. Walk the full lifecycle of a resource, not just how to create it. Pair every request with a real example response. Call out where the API behaves in a way a developer wouldn't expect. A developer guide is where the gap between who wrote the docs and who reads them shows up most. The team that built the API knows you can't really delete a driver, that eldSettings is read-only, and that the list defaults to active only. The developer reading doesn't, until something breaks. Samsara's guide works because it writes those down. Whatever you're documenting, the most useful thing you can do is hand the reader what only you currently know. How ReadMe Helps You Build Documentation Worth Using as an Example The fastest way for good documentation to go bad is to let it fall out of sync with the API. The code ships a change, the docs don't, and the gap between what's written and what's true starts widening with every release. Static files almost guarantee it, because keeping them current depends on someone remembering to. That drift is what turns docs developers trust into docs they learn to ignore. ReadMe builds interactive technical documents in minutes. Import a spec file to generate an API Reference automatically, or build one from scratch in the API designer, and developers get a page they can make real calls from, not a static file that goes stale the moment your API changes. Keeping docs current as they grow is the harder problem, and it's the one ReadMe is designed around. The Linter and Docs Audit flag errors and style drift as you write and track quality across the whole site, while the GitHub AI Writer drafts doc updates when your code changes, so your docs follow the API instead of falling behind it. Companies like Socure, Gusto, Clever, and Doppler already run on ReadMe. Socure shaved 30% off developer onboarding by rebuilding their docs around AI-powered search and discovery. Gusto runs two distinct APIs out of a single hub, without losing the compliance context developers need. Clever brought the same hands-on support their enterprise customers get to everyone else. Doppler replaced a homegrown docs setup with ReadMe and cut support tickets by more than a third. You can get started on our platform for free today, or book a call with our sales team to see how ReadMe can help you turn your technical documents into one of these prime examples. FAQs If you’re looking for more advice on upgrading your technical docs, refer to these common questions. How can I improve my API documentation? The best way to improve your API documentation is to add code examples and their respective returns, explain errors and how to fix them, and use clear, detailed language. It’s also important to keep your technical docs updated regularly. Finally, you might consider transitioning static docs to interactive ones that enable developers to test on the page. What does an API reference doc need? An API reference doc needs to include endpoints, parameters, and response codes for interacting with your API. It may also address common errors and use cases with code examples. What is a good example of technical documentation? A good example of technical documentation is one that's written for the developer reading it, not the team that built the API. Strong examples, like the Gusto and Samsara guides covered above, share a few traits: they explain what something does before diving into detail, show real code and example responses, and flag the places where developers commonly get stuck. The best technical documentation examples reduce support tickets by answering questions before they're asked. What are the main types of technical documentation? The main types of technical documentation for an API are the API reference, getting started guide, tutorial, changelog, and developer guide. The reference documents every endpoint and parameter, the getting started guide walks a new developer to their first call, tutorials teach a specific task end-to-end, the changelog tracks what's changed, and the developer guide covers the full lifecycle of working with a resource. Most strong developer docs include all five.

title: BBVA Mexico SWIFT code: How to find and use it
summary: Need the BBVA Mexico SWIFT code for an international transfer? Here is the code, how to find it, and how to use it to send or receive money. Read on.
body_text: Trying to send money to a BBVA account in Mexico without the SWIFT code is like trying to mail a package without an address. A SWIFT code is a short combination of letters and numbers that informs the international banking system exactly where your money needs to go. The SWIFT code for BBVA Mexico (BBVA Bancomer) is BCMRMXMM, used to route international transfers to a BBVA account in Mexico. You need it, along with the recipient's account number or CLABE, to send money from abroad. Always confirm the code with the recipient or BBVA before sending. BBVA Mexico SWIFT/BIC code: BCMRMXMM If you are sending money internationally to a BBVA Mexico account, whether to pay a supplier, support family, or settle a personal transaction, you need this code to route the transfer correctly. This guide explains what the code means, how to find it yourself, and what else you need to complete a successful transfer. What is the BBVA Mexico SWIFT code? BBVA Mexico is Mexico’s largest financial institution, established in 1932 with its headquarters in Mexico City. It is the most profitable overseas subsidiary of BBVA Spain, its parent institution. BBVA Mexico's SWIFT/BIC code is BCMRMXMM You may also see it written as BCMRMXMMXXX , where the XXX identifies the head office. Both formats can be accepted for international transfers. A SWIFT code is also called a Bank Identifier Code (BIC). It refers to an 8 to 11-character code that identifies a bank when sending money internationally. It tells the sending bank where to send the transfer. It may also specify the branch and location to route the transfer to. BBVA Mexico was formerly known as BBVA Bancomer until 2019, when the bank rebranded. However, the SWIFT code BCMRMXMM remained unchanged after the rebranding. Only the bank’s name changed from BBVA Bancomer to BBVA Mexico, S.A. So, if you see older documentation referencing "BBVA Bancomer," the SWIFT code shown there is still valid. BBVA Mexico's code (BCMRMXMM) is different from BBVA Spain’s code (BBVAESMMXXX). These are separate entities, even though BBVA Spain is the parent institution. If you're sending money to a Mexican BBVA account, use the Mexico-specific code. If you use BBVA Spain’s code instead, your money will be routed to the wrong account and may not be recoverable. How to find the SWIFT code yourself If you're unsure which SWIFT code to use, you can check: Through online or mobile banking: If you or the recipient has access to BBVA Mexico's online banking or mobile app, the SWIFT/BIC code is usually listed under account details or international transfer information. On a bank statement: Some BBVA Mexico statements include the SWIFT code with your account information. On BBVA's official website: Check BBVA Mexico's website to confirm the current SWIFT codes for international transfers. Directly from the recipient: If you're sending money to someone with a BBVA Mexico account, ask them to confirm their banking details before making the transfer. Some branches may have an extended SWIFT code. SWIFT code vs CLABE: what is the difference? If you're sending money to a BBVA Mexico account, you may need both the SWIFT code and CLABE, but they serve different purposes. The SWIFT code (BCMRMXMM) identifies the bank in Mexico that receives the payment and how to route the transfer from the sending bank to BBVA Mexico. Think of it as the bank's international address that tells the international banking network where to send the money. The CLABE (Clave Bancaria Estandarizada) is an 18-digit standardised interbank code unique to Mexico. It is required for all electronic transfers within the Mexican banking system. It identifies the specific account within BBVA Mexico where the funds should be paid. Think of it as identifying the specific mailbox at the address the SWIFT code points you to. For an international wire transfer to a BBVA Mexico account, you generally need both the SWIFT code to route the transfer to the correct bank and the CLABE to ensure the funds land in the correct account. How to use it to send or receive money Once you have the recipient's details, sending the money is straightforward. Step 1: Confirm all the recipient's details You need the recipient's full legal name, their CLABE (18 digits), the SWIFT code (BCMRMXMM, or the specific branch code if provided), and the bank's name and address. Step 2: Initiate the transfer through your bank Log in to your bank's online platform or visit a branch. Select international wire transfer and enter the recipient's details exactly as provided, including the SWIFT code and CLABE. Step 3: Enter the details Enter the recipient's information exactly as provided. Double-check the SWIFT code and CLABE before continuing. Step 4: Confirm the transfer currency Depending on your bank and the recipient's account, you may be able to send USD or MXN. Confirm which currency the recipient expects before sending. Step 5: Review fees before confirming Your sending bank will typically charge an outgoing wire fee, commonly $25 to $50 for international wires from US banks. Correspondent banks in the routing chain may deduct additional fees before the funds reach BBVA Mexico. Step 6: Track the transfer Save the transfer reference your bank provides so you can track the payment if there is a delay. Many banks now support SWIFT GPI tracking, which shows where the transfer is in the routing chain and its estimated arrival time. International wire transfers to Mexico typically take 1 to 5 business days, depending on the sending bank, the currency, and whether the transfer passes through one or more correspondent banks. If you regularly send to Mexico, opening a multi-currency account can simplify the process rather than using international wires each time. You can hold money in your preferred currency before converting it for a transfer to Mexico. A cheaper way to send money to Mexico Traditional SWIFT transfers can come with several fees. Your bank may charge an outgoing wire fee, correspondent banks may deduct undisclosed fees along the way, and the exchange rate may include an additional 1-5% markup. These costs can reduce the amount your recipient receives. Sending money from the US to Mexico with Grey offers a transparent alternative. You can see the exchange rate and transfer fee before confirming, so you know how much your recipient will receive in Mexican pesos. This is particularly useful for regular transfers, whether supporting family, paying a Mexican contractor, or handling personal finances across the two countries. If you're planning a trip and sending money, our guide on the best time to visit Mexico covers weather, seasons, and money tips. Send money to Mexico with Grey and avoid international wire fees, correspondent bank charges, and hidden exchange-rate markups. Frequently asked questions about BBVA Mexico’s SWIFT code What is BBVA Mexico's SWIFT code? BBVA Mexico's SWIFT/BIC code is BCMRMXMM, sometimes shown as BCMRMXMMXXX. This code identifies BBVA Mexico's head office for international wire transfers. Some branches may have extended codes (such as BCMRMXMMPYM), so it's always best to confirm with the recipient before sending. Is BBVA the same as Bancomer? Yes, in the sense that BBVA Mexico was formerly branded as BBVA Bancomer before a 2019 rebrand. It is the same institution with the same SWIFT code (BCMRMXMM) as before the name change. If you have older documentation or contacts referencing "Bancomer," the bank details remain accurate; only the name has updated. Do I need the CLABE too? Yes. The SWIFT code alone routes your transfer to BBVA Mexico as an institution, but it does not identify a specific account. The 18-digit CLABE (Clave Bancaria Estandarizada) identifies the exact account the funds should be credited to. Both are required for a complete and accurate international transfer to a Mexican bank account. How long does a transfer take? International wire transfers to BBVA Mexico typically take one to five business days, depending on your sending bank, the currency used, and whether the transfer passes through one or more correspondent banks in transit. Transfers sent through platforms using local payment networks rather than the full SWIFT correspondent chain can settle faster. What are the fees? Standard SWIFT wires from US banks typically incur an outgoing fee of $25 to $50, plus potential correspondent bank deductions of $15 to $30 in transit, and a currency conversion margin if the transfer is converted to Mexican pesos, generally 1% to 5% above the mid-market rate. These costs are not always fully disclosed before you send. Is there a cheaper alternative to a SWIFT wire? Yes. Platforms like Grey process international transfers with fees and exchange rates disclosed before you confirm. They often route payments through local payment networks rather than the traditional SWIFT correspondent-bank chain. This avoids the additional costs of a standard bank wire. This is often a cheaper alternative to a SWIFT wire, especially for regular transfers to Mexico.

title: BMW M2 Buying Guide: Cost, Reliability, and the Best Years to Buy
summary: Our definitive BMW M2 buying guide covers the history and specs of the two model generations available, how much you can expect to pay for one, and which are the best and worst versions to buy.
body_text: The BMW M2 hit the scene in 2016 as a successor to the limited run of 1 M Coupe models that the German automaker launched in 2011. Spiritually, the new M2 went back to BMW’s roots as a rear-wheel-drive, M-badged car that prioritized fun handling over outright performance. But that doesn’t mean the M2 wasn’t a proper sports coupe, as evidenced by its 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-six engine that produced 365 horsepower. The 2016 BMW M2 competed with the likes of the Audi S3 and RS3 and the Mercedes-AMG CLA Series. Buyers may also have considered the Cadillac ATS-V sedan, but that was a bit pricier and had two additional doors. In any case, the M2 reinvigorated BMW’s old mantra of delivering the Ultimate Driving Machine with a refreshing combination of performance, attainability, and style. Bigger and more powerful than the first generation, the latest version stands out as a true driver’s car for buyers who value performance and don’t need the practicality of a four-door sedan. BMW M2 Buying Guide: Cost, Reliability, and the Best Years to Buy Frequently Asked Questions Pros and Cons BMW M2 Generations BMW M2 Second Generation (2023-Present) BMW M2 First Generation (2016-2022) Frequently Asked Questions Which BMW M2 years are the best? The BMW M2 has very few known reliability issues, with CarComplaints.com citing 2023 as the worst year overall, even though it only has one complaint. J.D. Power consistently rates the BMW 2 Series line as one of the most reliable coupes available in the United States, although the M2 has more power, more equipment, and different options than the rest of its 2 Series Coupe siblings. Considering its status as a high-performance machine, buyers shopping for used BMW M2 models should consider having any vehicle they are considering checked over by a qualified mechanic. A long list of proper scheduled maintenance is also valuable. Which BMW M2 years are the worst? Early BMW M2 models used older iDrive infotainment technology that is now outdated and less intuitive than modern systems. On the reliability front, though, there aren’t any specific model years to avoid. How much does a late-model BMW M2 cost? Used M2 values remain strong. A 1-year-old 2025 BMW M2 averages around $71,800, while a 3-year-old 2023 model averages around $65,800. These figures reflect robust used-market demand for the compact sports coupe. Research BMW M2 Price Trends on CarGurus Is a used BMW M2 a good deal? Considering its solid reliability, desirability, and excellent residual values, a used BMW M2 could be considered a good deal. There is a premium to pay, but it’s a premium product. Used M2 prices are up about 18% year over year, well ahead of roughly 2% for the broader CarGurus used-car market, underscoring strong value retention. According to CarGurus used car pricing data , used BMW M2 prices vary from a little less than $40,000 for early first-generation models all the way up to around $71,800 for low-mileage, nearly new examples. For that, buyers could choose an American muscle car such as the Ford Mustang Shelby GT350 or a Chevrolet Corvette from 2014-2019. Other competitors, such as the Audi TT RS and the Mercedes-AMG CLA45, don’t offer a traditional rear-wheel-drive platform but do provide plenty of performance. Pros and Cons Pros: Powerful engine Manual transmission available Fun to drive Cons: Stiff ride in normal driving Bit of effort to enter/exit Styling is not for everyone BMW M2 Generations BMW M2 Second Generation (2023–Present) The second and current generation of the BMW M2 debuted for the 2023 model year. It’s 4.1 inches longer and 1.3 inches wider than the first generation and has more power, but it’s still compact and combines true driving appeal with daily-driver practicality. The 14-cubic-foot trunk is large for a coupe, the rear seat is fine for two adults, and the two front occupants have plenty of room. However, it isn’t the easiest vehicle to enter or exit due to its aggressively bolstered M Sport front seats—and the optional M Carbon bucket seats are even more restrictive. Those, along with a stiff ride, are the necessary drawbacks of a thrilling sports coupe. When it was introduced, the 2023 M2’s twin-turbo 3.0-liter inline-six engine produced 453 horsepower and 406 pound-feet of torque, all routed to the rear wheels through either a six-speed manual transmission with a high-tech rev matching system, or an eight-speed automatic with steering-wheel-mounted paddle shifters. A computer-controlled Active M limited-slip differential was standard and, regardless of transmission, 0-60 was dispatched in less than four seconds. While fuel economy isn’t as important as outright horsepower in this type of vehicle, the EPA estimates of 16 mpg in the city, 24 mpg on the highway, and 19 mpg combined (drop one highway mpg for the automatic transmission) aren’t much to write home about. The second-generation M2 has more visual flair than the first, with a bespoke, muscular look. A wider stance is accentuated by bulging wheel arches, while the front fascia’s blocky air openings include BMW’s kidney-shaped grilles, a lower intake and two large squared-off intakes. Under the skin, a stiff chassis with near 50:50 weight distribution means the M2 is designed to excel at the race track or on the road. BMW’s Adaptive M Suspension is standard, featuring electronically controlled dampers that adjust on the move with split-second precision. Powerful brakes and a stability control system with 10 settings prove that BMW intended the M2 to be driven hard. Inside, there’s the manufacturer’s “Curved Display” layout, with a digital gauge cluster and a large touchscreen infotainment screen running BMW’s iDrive 8 operating system. Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are supported, while a Harman Kardon audio system is a nice standard feature. Dynamic cruise control, forward-collision warning with brake assist, lane-departure warning, and park-assist with sensors at the front and rear came standard with the 2023 M2, while active cruise control with stop and go was optional. Though the M2 wasn’t tested separately from the rest of the 2 Series lineup, the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) gave the entire line its highest rating in all of its crash tests. BMW offered just one trim level but several optional packages for the 2023 M2. An M Driver’s Package included one day at a high-performance driving school and increased the car’s speed limit from 155 mph to 177 mph. A Lighting Package added adaptive headlights and high-beam assist, while a Shadowline Package added dark exterior accents. A Carbon Package added a carbon fiber roof that provided a slight performance advantage, along with carbon interior trim, the extra-tight carbon bucket seats, black wheels, and the M Driver’s Package. The 2024 M2 didn’t get any meaningful updates, but BMW increased the turbocharged engine’s power from 453 to 473 horsepower for 2025. The infotainment system was also updated from iDrive 8.0 to iDrive 8.5 that year, although not all owners appreciated the move from physical climate controls to virtual touchscreen buttons. The BMW M2 CS was launched for 2026, adding 50 hp and 36 lb-ft, bringing the totals to 523 hp and 479 lb-ft. The CS, which stands for Competition Sport, also weighs about 100 pounds less than the regular M2 thanks to the use of carbon fiber for the roof, the trunk lid (which features a large ducktail spoiler), the side mirror caps, and the rear diffuser. The CS comes solely with an automatic transmission. For 2027, BMW added its xDrive all-wheel-drive system to the M2 for the first time. The system prioritizes rear-wheel-drive dynamics, sending power to the front wheels only when it detects rear-wheel slip. The M2 xDrive comes exclusively with an eight-speed automatic transmission, though BMW still offers the M2 with a six-speed manual and rear-wheel drive. Under the hood, the standard twin-turbo 3.0-liter inline-six produces 473 horsepower and 443 pound-feet of torque. BMW says the xDrive model reaches 60 mph in 3.6 seconds, 0.3 seconds quicker than the rear-wheel-drive version. Top speed is 155 mph, or 177 mph with the M Driver’s Package. A new Borusan Turkish Blue paint color rounds out the 2027 updates. At the time of writing, the 2026 BMW M2 started at $70,350 (including a mandatory destination charge). Some paint colors can add up to $3,000 to the price, while the Carbon Package tacks on a hefty $9,900. BMW says the 2027 M2 goes on sale in late summer 2026, with the M2 xDrive starting at $74,950 including destination; rear-wheel-drive versions are expected to cost less. Buyers looking to save some money by purchasing a low-mileage used second-generation BMW M2 will find that prices start around $65,800 according to CarGurus used car pricing data . BMW M2 First Generation (2016–2022) Seeing the success that it had with the limited-edition 1 M Coupe, BMW followed that well-loved machine with the M2 coupe in 2016. Although based on the platform of the regular 2 Series model, the M2 has all the upgrades fans would associate with a BMW M model. Power comes from a turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-six engine tuned to deliver 365 hp and 369 lb-ft of torque, making the 2016 BMW M2 properly quick. And with its standard six-speed manual transmission or optional seven-speed automatic dual-clutch transmission (DCT) and rear-wheel-drive chassis, it became a favorite for enthusiasts looking for some daily-driving fun. As is typical of an M-badged BMW, the M2 had more than just a punched-up engine. BMW fitted the 2016 M2 with big brakes and 19-inch wheels wearing sticky Michelin Pilot Super Sport tires, while the exterior bodywork package added a few extra inches of width, a rear-lip spoiler, and quad exhaust tips. The 2016 BMW M2’s upgraded front seats and carbon fiber trim extended the sporty look into the cabin. An 8.8-inch infotainment screen required inputs from a console-mounted rotary knob. The 2016 BMW M2 with a manual transmission was rated by the EPA to deliver 18 mpg in the city, 26 mpg on the highway, and 21 mpg combined. The DCT delivered 20 mpg city, 27 mpg highway, and 23 mpg combined. Likely more important to buyers was the M2’s 0-60 time of 4.3 seconds with the manual or 4.1 seconds with the DCT. With its fancy M rear differential and selectable Comfort, Sport, and Sport+ modes, the 2016 M2 was also designed to deliver excellent handling and roadholding. BMW equipped the 2016 M2 with its Driving Assistant safety suite, which included forward-collision warning, pedestrian warning with a city braking function, and lane-departure warning. The 2016 BMW 2 Series was awarded the highest Top Safety Pick+ designation from the IIHS. BMW added Apple CarPlay (but not Android Auto) connectivity as an option in 2017, and an M Driver Package included a one-day trip to a performance driving school. For 2018, an updated iDrive infotainment system could be operated with a touchscreen display. The BMW M2 Competition model hit the market for the 2019 model year, bringing with it a new turbocharged engine bumped to 405 hp and 406 lb-ft. To go with the newfound power, BMW stiffened the M2’s chassis for 2019, retuned its suspension and electronic driver aids, upsized its brakes and refreshed its exterior bodywork. M Sport seats with more side bolstering were also newly optional. For 2020, BMW built a limited-edition M2 CS model with 444 hp, M Adaptive suspension, and optional carbon ceramic brakes and Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 tires. Carbon fiber exterior components reduced the CS model’s weight and increased performance. There weren’t any major changes for the first-generation M2 in its last couple of model years. According to CarGurus used pricing data , it’s possible to find first-generation BMW M2 models for less than $40,000. Later first-generation models can cost up to around $61,300, and M2 CS models are quite rare and therefore much pricier. title: How to Choose a Background Verification Company in India: The 2026 Buyer’s Checklist Every HR Manager Needs
summary: Learn how to choose the best background verification company in India with this 2026 checklist covering cost, speed, and security.
body_text: Insights & Resources How to Choose a Background Verification Company in India: The 2026 Buyer’s Checklist Every HR Manager Needs August 12, 2026 Shashank Yadav No comments yet You have decided that your company needs background verification. Maybe a bad hire cost you money. Maybe a client contract requires it. Maybe the DPDP Act 2023 made you realize that unverified employees handling personal data is a compliance risk you cannot afford. Now comes the hard part: choosing which verification company to use. A quick Google search returns dozens of options. Large agencies with enterprise sales teams. Digital startups promising instant results. Regional firms with local expertise. International companies with global databases. Every one of them claims to be the best, the fastest, the most affordable, and the most comprehensive. How do you actually evaluate these options? What questions should you ask? What features matter and what features are just marketing? How do you avoid signing a contract that locks you into a service that does not fit your needs? This guide gives you a structured evaluation framework. We have distilled the selection process into a practical checklist that covers every dimension that matters: technology, accuracy, speed, pricing, compliance, and support. Use this checklist to compare providers side by side, ask the right questions during vendor evaluations, and make a decision you will not regret. The 10 Point Evaluation Checklist 1. Does It Check Against Government Databases Directly? This is the single most important technical question. There are two fundamentally different approaches to document verification in India. API based verification sends the document number directly to the relevant government database (Income Tax Department for PAN, Election Commission for Voter ID, VAHAN/SARATHI for Driving Licence, EPFO for UAN) and receives an authoritative response. The result comes from the source of truth. It cannot be fooled by a forged document because it does not look at the document. It checks the number against the database. Manual or field agent verification involves a person visually inspecting the document and making a judgment about whether it appears genuine. This approach cannot detect AI generated forgeries, digitally altered certificates, or sophisticated fakes that look identical to real documents. In 2026, API based verification is the standard for identity checks. Any provider that relies primarily on visual document inspection for PAN, Voter ID, or Driving Licence verification is using an obsolete approach that misses the most common forms of modern document fraud. What to ask the provider: “Do you verify PAN, Voter ID, and Driving Licence through direct API integrations with government databases, or through manual document inspection?” 2. How Fast Are Results? Speed matters for two reasons. First, candidates with multiple offers will accept the employer who confirms fastest. A two week verification delay loses you talent. Second, roles that need to be filled urgently (seasonal hiring, replacement hires, growth phase onboarding) cannot wait for traditional timelines. Benchmark for 2026: Identity checks (PAN, Voter ID, Driving Licence) should return results in minutes, not days. Any provider quoting 24 to 48 hours for a PAN check is using manual processes that add unnecessary delay. UAN employment history should return within minutes to a few hours for digital platforms. Criminal record checks take 24 to 72 hours through digital eCourts database searches. Physical court visits take 7 to 14 business days. Education verification takes 3 to 15 business days depending on institutional response times. This is the one area where speed is largely outside the provider’s control. What to ask the provider: “What is the turnaround time for each check type? Specifically, how long does a PAN or Voter ID verification take?” 3. Does It Offer Cross Record Analysis? A single document check tells you whether that one document is valid. Cross record analysis compares details across multiple documents and highlights inconsistencies. For example, if the PAN card returns “Amit Kumar, born 15 June 1992” and the Voter ID returns “Amit Kumar Singh, born 16 June 1992,” a single document check would show both as valid. Cross record analysis flags the name variation and the date of birth discrepancy, prompting further investigation. Without cross record analysis, your HR team must manually compare details across every document for every candidate. This is time consuming and error prone. What to ask the provider: “Do you offer automatic cross record analysis when multiple documents are verified for the same candidate? Is this included in the price or charged separately?” 4. What Does the Pricing Structure Look Like? Pricing structures in the Indian verification market vary widely. Understanding the structure is as important as understanding the price. Pay per check (no subscription): You pay only for checks you run. No monthly fees, no annual contracts, no minimum volumes. Best for companies with variable hiring patterns. Subscription with included checks: Monthly or annual fee includes a set number of checks. Overages are charged at a higher rate. Best for companies with predictable, consistent volume. Annual contract with volume commitment: Custom pricing based on committed annual volume. Penalties or wasted spend if you do not meet the commitment. Red flags in pricing: Platform access fees charged on top of per check prices. Rush processing surcharges for faster results (digital platforms should not need this because all results are fast). Separate charges for PDF report generation. Setup or integration fees. Minimum volume requirements that do not match your actual hiring pattern. Prices that are only revealed after a sales call. What to ask the provider: “Is the per check price all inclusive, or are there additional fees for platform access, report generation, rush processing, or setup? Is there a minimum volume commitment?” 5. Can You See the Price Before You Pay? This seems basic, but many verification providers require you to talk to a sales representative before revealing their pricing. They want to qualify you as a lead, understand your volume, and negotiate a custom price. In 2026, pricing opacity is a red flag. The best platforms show you the exact price for each check before you complete the transaction. You know what you are paying before you commit. What to ask the provider: “Can I see the complete price for each check on your website or platform before talking to a sales representative? Is the quoted price the final price, or are there additional charges?” 6. How Good Are the Reports? A verification result is only useful if your HR team can understand and act on it. Evaluate the report quality on these dimensions. Clarity. Are statuses clearly labeled (verified, mismatch, unable to verify)? Can a non specialist understand what each result means? Completeness. Does the report show what was checked, what the government database returned, and whether the returned details match the candidate’s claims? Format. Is the report available as a downloadable PDF? Can it be attached to the employee’s file for compliance and audit purposes? Consistency. Are reports structured the same way for every candidate, making it easy to compare results across multiple verifications? Delivery. Are reports delivered automatically (by email or through the platform), or do you have to request them separately? What to ask the provider: “Can I see a sample report before signing up? Are PDF reports included in the price, or charged separately?” 7. Is the Platform Self Serve? The verification industry has historically operated on a relationship model: you talk to a sales representative, sign a contract, and submit verification requests through an account manager. This model works for large enterprises but adds unnecessary friction for smaller companies. Self serve platforms let you create an account, enter candidate details, select checks, pay, and get results without ever talking to a sales representative. This is faster, simpler, and gives you complete control over your verification process. What to ask the provider: “Can I create an account and run my first check without talking to a sales representative or signing a contract?” ID Verify by SalaryBox (compose1.com/verify) is fully self serve. No sales calls, no demos, no contracts. Create an account and run a check when you need one. 8. How Does It Handle Data Security? Background verification involves sensitive personal data: PAN numbers, Voter ID numbers, dates of birth, employment histories, and criminal records. How the provider handles this data matters. Account bound access. Verification data should be visible only to the account holder who initiated the check. Shared dashboards where multiple users can see all verifications create unnecessary data exposure. Masked identifiers. Sensitive document numbers should be masked until the appropriate point in the workflow. Displaying full PAN or Voter ID numbers throughout the process is a data security risk. Secure checkout. Payment processing should use industry standard encryption. Your payment details should never be stored on the verification platform. Data retention policies. The provider should have clear policies on how long verification data is retained and how it is eventually deleted. What to ask the provider: “Where is verification data stored? Who can access it? Are document numbers masked during the workflow? What is your data retention policy?” 9. What Is the Coverage? Coverage has two dimensions: geographic and check type. Geographic coverage. For Indian companies hiring Indian candidates, the key question is whether the provider checks against national databases. PAN, Voter ID, Driving Licence, and UAN are national databases, so any provider with API access covers the entire country. For criminal record checks, coverage depends on which courts and jurisdictions are included in the search. Check type coverage. Evaluate whether the provider offers the specific checks you need. Most companies need some combination of identity verification (PAN, Voter ID, Driving Licence), employment history (UAN), criminal record checks, education verification, and address verification. What to ask the provider: “Which government databases do you have API access to? For criminal record checks, which states and districts are covered?” 10. What Happens When Something Goes Wrong? Even the best verification platforms occasionally encounter issues: a government database is temporarily unavailable, a check returns an unexpected result, or a candidate disputes a finding. Customer support. Is support available by email, chat, or phone? What is the typical response time? Is support included in the price, or is it a premium add on? Failed checks. What happens when a check returns “unable to verify” due to a technical issue? Is the retry free, or do you pay again? Dispute resolution. If a candidate disputes a verification finding, does the provider assist with resolution? What to ask the provider: “What happens if a check fails due to a database being unavailable? Am I charged for failed checks? How do you handle candidate disputes?” Comparing Provider Types Large Traditional Agencies Examples include AuthBridge, First Advantage, and HireRight. Strengths. Comprehensive check types including physical verification, global coverage for multinational companies, established processes for regulated industries. Weaknesses. Slower turnaround (7 to 21 days standard), higher costs (Rs 1,500 to Rs 5,000 per candidate for standard packages), annual contracts with volume minimums, require sales calls to get started. Best for. Large enterprises with predictable high volumes, regulated industries requiring comprehensive screening, and companies needing global coverage. Digital API Based Platforms Examples include ID Verify by SalaryBox (compose1.com/verify), and other digital first providers. Strengths. Instant to same day results for identity checks, significantly lower per check costs, self serve access with no sales calls, pay per check pricing with no minimums, government database API verification that catches document fraud. Weaknesses. May not offer physical address verification through field agents, limited reference interview capabilities, some specialized checks (CIBIL, directorship) may not be available on all platforms. Best for. SMEs, startups, companies with variable hiring volumes, frontline and operational hiring, and any organization that values speed and cost efficiency. Regional or Niche Agencies Smaller agencies with specialization in specific regions or industries. Strengths. Local knowledge, personal service, sometimes better reach in specific geographic areas for physical verification. Weaknesses. Limited technology, inconsistent quality, may not have API access to government databases, limited scalability. Best for. Companies with very specific local verification needs that national providers cannot address. The Recommended Approach for Most Indian Companies For the majority of Indian companies in 2026, the optimal approach is a combination of digital and traditional verification. For every hire (digital, through ID Verify): Run PAN, Voter ID, Driving Licence, and UAN checks through a digital API based platform. These are the most commonly needed checks, they are the most affordable through digital platforms, and they return the fastest results. Cross record analysis catches identity inconsistencies automatically. For selected hires (traditional, through an agency): Engage a traditional agency for checks that genuinely require human involvement. Criminal record deep dives in specific courts, physical address verification, detailed reference interviews, and credit checks for financial roles. This approach gives you speed and affordability for 90 percent of your verification needs while maintaining comprehensive screening for the roles that warrant it. Getting Started with ID Verify If you are ready to start verifying candidates, here is the fastest path. Step 1: Visit compose1.com/verify and create an account. No sales calls, no contracts, no setup fees. Step 2: Start a verification. Enter the candidate’s details and select the checks you need. Step 3: See the price, confirm, and pay securely. Step 4: Review results as they complete. Download the PDF report. Store verification records in your private workspace. The entire process from account creation to first verification result takes minutes. You will have a verified candidate report before a traditional agency would have even assigned a field agent. Frequently Asked Questions Should I choose a large agency or a digital platform? For identity and employment verification (PAN, Voter ID, DL, UAN), digital platforms are faster, cheaper, and more accurate. For comprehensive checks including physical verification and detailed references, large agencies add value. Many companies use both: digital for most hires, agency for senior roles. How do I know if a provider actually uses government database APIs? Ask directly: “Do you verify PAN through the Income Tax Department API?” If the answer involves field agents, document scanning, or visual inspection, they are not using API based verification. API based results arrive in minutes. Manual results take days. What is a reasonable cost per candidate for a growing company? For identity verification (PAN and Voter ID), Rs 100 to Rs 400 per candidate through a digital platform is reasonable. For a full identity plus employment history check, Rs 300 to Rs 600 is fair. If you are paying more than Rs 1,000 per candidate for basic identity checks, you are overpaying. Do I need background verification if I only have 5 employees? Yes. One bad hire in a 5 person company affects 20 percent of your workforce. And with pay per check platforms like ID Verify, the cost of verifying 5 employees is negligible. There is no minimum order to worry about. Can I switch providers mid contract? If you are on a pay per check platform with no contract, you can switch at any time. If you are locked into an annual contract, review the termination clauses. This is another reason to prefer pay per check models: no switching costs. Is there a free trial available? Pricing models vary by provider. With ID Verify’s pay per check model, you do not need a trial. Your first check costs the same as your hundredth. There is no commitment to evaluate. Choose Once. Verify Confidently. The right verification partner saves your company time, money, and hiring risk. The wrong one locks you into contracts you do not need, charges for overhead you did not ask for, and delivers results too slowly to keep up with your hiring.
